newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees die, fighters said to take Zaire children.
newsitem.headline: Refugees die, fighters said to take Zaire children.

text.p: Zairean villagers said on Thursday Rwandan Hutu fighters seized their children as hostages in east Zaire's war zone and U.N. officials reported refugees dying of thirst.

The first Zaireans fleeing a Tutsi offensive arrived with swollen feet in a city more than 500 km (300 miles) from their homes and in Kinshasa students took over parliament briefly, demanding the fall of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
Two mothers in Keshero village near Goma told Reuters they lost 12 children to Rwandan Hutu kidnappers and the director of a local school said about 100 children in all had been taken.
The last foreign aid workers in eastern Zaire fled the Goma area last week so no independent confirmation was available.
"The Interahamwe came to our house on Saturday. They forced my family to leave the village and took all eight of my children with them as hostages to Mugunga camp," said Suzanne Damukunzi.
The Interahamwe extremist Hutu militiamen had a leading role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates and are fighting the advancing Tutsi rebels.
Elisabeth Huyimana said Rwandan Hutus, living in camps for two years before war between Tutsi rebels and Zairean forces broke out nearly three weeks ago, came to her home on Sunday.
"They took four of my children with them as hostage," she said. After the abductions, Keshero was taken by Tutsi forces.
"Around 100 children have been taken to Mugunga from here," school director Evariste Mkundiye told Reuters.
Keshero is eight km (five miles) from Goma and across a frontline just two km (one mile) from Mugunga camp, home for 400,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees including Interahamwe militiamen.
"They (Interhamwe fighters) want to make us know that we will all have to die together," orphanage manager Floribert Makongo said. "They are turning Mugunga into a hostage camp."

Despite a one-sided ceasefire declared by the rebels on Monday, mortars and anti-aircraft gunfire were heard from the area north of Mugunga as night fell and eyewitnesses said fighting raged earlier on Thursday along the frontline.
In Brussels, ministers of the European Union, pilloried for inaction in the Zaire crisis, said they were ready to do all they could but only agreed to dispatch a new fact-finding team.
EU aid chief Emma Bonino stressed it was up to the U.N. Security Council to create conditions necessary for aid work to resume. "We can go tomorrow...only we are forbidden," she said.
But France and Spain remained isolated in their drive to send their forces in a U.N.-backed force to ensure security for aid distribution. Ethiopia has also offered to contribute.
The Spanish foreign ministry said on Wednesday Spain and France wanted to send a force of 5,000 soldiers but would only go ahead if the United States and United Nations backed it.
In the latest anti-government protest in Kinshasa, students carrying coffins of two dead colleagues flooded the parliament building but later dispersed. Security forces did not intervene.
The first 50 Zairean men and women trekked into the Zairean city of Kisangani, sick, with swollen feet and their belongings gone, and said hundreds more were behind them, an aid worker said.

"We have no means of taking care of them -- no food, no medicine. It's a catastrophe," Claude Olenga, administrator of the church charity CARITAS, told Reuters in Kisangani, the last major Zairean outpost before a vast stretch of hills and jungle.
Olenga said the 50 said they left from Bukavu, 530 km (330 miles) southeast of Kisangani and taken by rebels last week.
Rwandan refugees arriving in the Rwandan town of Gisenyi bordering on rebel-held Goma city told U.N. officials of many deaths in the waterless, volcanic mountains north of Lake Kivu.

"They said they saw people dying all around them due to lack of water on the escarpment above Kahindo and Katale camps. One man was sucking water out of tree roots," said Peter Kessler, Nairobi spokesman of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.
Aid agencies have been ringing alarm bells about the 1.2 million refugees in eastern Zaire for weeks, but efforts to help have so far faded before the sheer complexities of the task.
Half the refugees are under the age of 16 and the part of east Zaire where they are dying is no longer in government hands.
It is held by an extraordinary medley of armies and militias acting out tribal and political rivalries, fuelled by land hunger, threatening to tear Zaire apart and doom the refugees.
On Wednesday Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko gave his support for an international intervention force for the east.
Mobutu, in France after treatment in Switzerland for cancer, has warmed to the French plan for an intervention force, hoping perhaps it might be a way to reassert his control in the east.
U.N. Envoy Raymond Chretien, who met Mobutu on Wednesday, arrived in Nairobi on Thursday and heads to Rwanda on Friday.
